newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - U.S. productivity seen up -- Rosenblum.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - U.S. productivity seen up -- Rosenblum.

text.p: The use of new technologies has made the output of goods and services more flexible, paving the way to an increase in productivity in the U.S. economy, said a top official at the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas.

"(The use of new technologies) has just made production of so many goods and so many services so much more flexible in ways that weren't possible a few years ago," Harvey Rosenblum, director of research at the Dallas Fed, told Reuters in an interview.
He said U.S. businesses have been adopting new technologies, such as newer and more powerful computer systems, very rapidly.

Such a phenomenon, he added, "has made an enormous difference in terms of the ability to keep the business growing (and) to add to capacity in ways that are difficult to measure by the usual standards."

Productivity gains have been a hot issue lately as economists, inside and outside the Federal Reserve, look for signs the nation can continue to grow rapidly with low unemployment without sparking higher inflation.
Rosenblum said the use of new technologies has been helping the economy for some time, but he believed its impact on the economy's productivity "may have accelerated in the last year or two."

The Dallas Fed director of research was a bit reluctant in fully embracing theories that the U.S. economy has created a "new paradigm," in which global competition and increased productivity were putting a permanent lid on price increases.
Rosenblum said, however, that "We are at a different world than we were in the 1970's.
"There's a different competitive environment, there is much more international competition than there was back then. There is a whole bunch of those kinds of things that re-inforce these trends."
Rosenblum also said increased competition has helped to keep inflation low.
"We talk to business around our region and what we keep hearing is: 'We're not able to raise prices.'

"Competitor pressures are keeping a hold on things. The good news is capacity seems to be expanding as fast as demand is expanding and that's kept a lid on price increases," the Dallas Fed director of research said.
So can this phenomenon persist for a prolonged period of time?

"As long as that trend stays in place, and of course you don't know how much longer it's going to stay in place, ... some of these positive productivity trends that we're getting throughout the economy are going to remain in place," he said.
Rosenblum also said he believes there is room for the unemployment rate -- currently hovering around five percent -- to drop further. Will that be a problem?
"Having more people working is never viewed as problem ... The real question is: Is their productivity going to match their wages?," Rosenblum said.
He said most productive people have already been drawn into the labor force, which is likely to force employers to recruit more marginal workers who might be less productive.
"Would that lead to inflation? Not necessarily but it certainly is not going to have the same impact of workers who were hired, say, three years ago on average," he said.

Although he did not want to disclose his estimates, Rosenblum said the U.S. economy was "rolling along," adding that he expected the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) numbers to show the economy slowed in the second quarter.
"I'm sure the numbers that will come out later this week will show it slowing down in the second quarter. But still, it's going to be pretty healthy rates of growth," he said.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1676 ))
